paras: The lynching of William A. Parker was the hanging of a white man by masked men from the river drawbridge at Washington, North Carolina, in March 1888, after they took him from the town lock-up. Parker had been tried and acquitted in the 1880 assassination of Gen. Bryan Grimes, and his killers left a placard reading "Justice at last." A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and papers as far away as Minnesota called him Grimes's murderer.

According to the Washington Gazette, Grimes was shot from the roadside near Bear Creek, five or six miles from Washington, on August 14, 1880. Parker was arraigned at the November court, and the case was later removed to Martin County, "where Parker was cleared." Several papers said he had since boasted of the killing when drinking; the Scotland Neck Democrat called him "the confessed murderer," while the State Chronicle wrote that this was "alleged."

On a Saturday in March Parker was in Washington, drinking and, the Gazette reported, again boasting that he had killed Grimes. About 7 o'clock he was placed, drunk, in the lock-up under the Town Hall in the charge of Rafe Long, the "colored night watch." At the inquest the keeper testified that about 2 a.m. the light went out and "at least half a dozen masked men" told him to keep quiet on pain of death. The Gazette put the number at a dozen or fifteen men, some masked, who shut the keeper in a cell, broke the lock on Parker's cell and took him out as he cried "Murder!"

About 3 a.m. the bridge keeper, opening the draw for the steamer Beta, found it obstructed by a rope from a crossbeam with a body at its end. Parker had been gagged, and the placard "Justice at Last" hung above his head; the body was left until daylight, and by 9 o'clock hundreds of people had gathered.

Arthur Mayo, appointed coroner, held an inquest at about 9:30, and his six-man jury found that Parker died "by hanging at the hands of persons unknown to the jury." Relatives removed the body for burial, and no report of an arrest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage. In May the Richmond Dispatch's North Carolina correspondent wrote that many Beaufort County residents believed corrupt jurors made "Judge Lynch" a necessity, citing "the Parker lynching in March."

The first report, a special from Washington to the Raleigh News and Observer, went out on the wire and appeared on March 13 and 14 in the Washington Evening Star, the Richmond Dispatch, the New York Sun and the New-York Tribune, among others. Headlines cast Parker as guilty: the Evening Star announced "The Murderer of Gen. Grimes Taken from Jail and Killed," and the Dispatch wrote of "Retribution" overtaking "a Self-Acknowledged Murderer." The wire text said only that he "was tried for" the assassination, and the Mower County Transcript in Minnesota stated flatly that he had "murdered General Bryan Grimes."

North Carolina papers more often noted the acquittal, and the Raleigh State Chronicle headed its item "The Alleged Murderer of Gen. Bryan Grimes Lynched." The Progressive Farmer called Parker "a white man, but of very disreputable character" and suggested the "vigilantes" had hanged him for "general cussedness." The Gazette called the deed "awful in itself" but reported few regrets at the bridge and the hope that it might "strike terror to the hearts of evil doers."

The Gazette and the Progressive Farmer placed the seizure on Saturday night, March 10, and the State Chronicle said the body was found on the morning of March 11. Other papers gave Sunday the 12th, March 12, or the 13th, following wire datelines, and the Washington Critic said Parker was arrested on a Monday. The Gazette, published in Washington and giving the hour-by-hour sequence, is the most direct source.

reader.title: Lynching of William A. Parker
bases: Masked men took Parker from the town lock-up and hanged him from the drawbridge with a placard reading 'Justice at last' (A1, A13).

Parker was hanged by at least half a dozen (local paper: a dozen or fifteen) masked men who broke him out of the lock-up, with no lawful authority (A1, A13); the placard 'Justice at last' and the reports tie the act to the 1880 killing of Gen. Grimes, for which he had been tried and acquitted (A14, A16).

The local Washington Gazette account (A13) and the separately written News and Observer special (A1, A14) agree on the seizure from the lock-up, the hanging from the drawbridge and the placard; other N.C. papers concur (A2, A16, A19).

accounts.gist: Awakened about 2 a.m., he found the light out and at least half a dozen masked men, who told him to keep quiet on pain of death, wrenched the lock off Parker's cell and carried him out.

accounts.label: Washington Gazette (local)
accounts.gist: At 2:10 a.m. nearby street lamps went out and a dozen or fifteen men, some masked, shut the keeper in a cell and took Parker, who cried 'Murder!' in the street; he was found gagged and hanged from the bridge draw about 3 a.m.

accounts.label: Progressive Farmer
accounts.gist: Parker, a disreputable white man believed to have killed Grimes but acquitted, was hanged by vigilantes who made no specific charge, probably for 'general cussedness'.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the News and Observer wire under headlines such as 'Lynched for an Old Crime. The Murderer of Gen. Grimes Taken from Jail and Killed.'
The Richmond Dispatch headed the wire 'Justice at Last' and 'Retribution Overtakes a Self-Acknowledged Murderer After Eight Years.'
The Washington Gazette called the deed 'awful in itself' but reported few regrets and the hope it would deter 'evil doers'.
The State Chronicle headed it 'The Alleged Murderer of Gen. Bryan Grimes Lynched' and noted the acquittal.
The Progressive Farmer called Parker 'of very disreputable character' and suggested the vigilantes hanged him for 'general cussedness'.
The Richmond Dispatch's N.C. correspondent listed it among the year's lynchings and reported local belief that corrupt juries made 'Judge Lynch' a necessity.
